Data story

What the book catalogue data does and doesn’t tell us

200 books · median price £36 · 36 categories

The short version

  • Half of all books cost between £22 and £46.
  • Higher-rated books do not cost more.
  • Category barely changes price: the differences are within noise.
  • Ratings are spread evenly across 1 to 5 stars.
  • Every scraped row was usable.

The evidence, one chart at a time

So what: There is no single 'typical' price: books are spread almost evenly from about £10 to £60. Pricing rules should therefore use bands, not a single average.

So what: No rating dominates: the split is statistically indistinguishable from even (p = 0.56). A star rating alone therefore separates books very little.

So what: Rank correlation between price and rating is ρ = +0.02 (adjusted p = 1.00): no reliable link. Do not use price as a stand-in for quality.

So what: Median prices overlap across categories (Kruskal-Wallis adjusted p = 1.00). A single price policy is defensible; category-specific rules are not supported by this data.

So what: Independence test: adjusted p = 1.00, Cramér's V = 0.11. Nothing here suggests a segment worth targeting.

So what: All usable books have complete detail fields.

What this means for decisions

  • Don’t price by rating. No reliable link between the two, so rating-based price tiers are unsupported.
  • One pricing policy is enough. Category does not meaningfully move price here.
  • Look for signal elsewhere. None of the relationships tested was reliable; additional variables (reviews, publication date) are needed.

How far to trust this

  • Observational data from one site at one moment: associations are not causes.
  • Significance uses Holm-adjusted p-values across the four tests shown, and effect sizes must also be non-trivial to be called notable.
  • Extreme prices are excluded from the distribution and heat-map views, not from the statistics on price vs rating or category.
Source: cleaned_books.csv. Charts: Matplotlib + Seaborn. Palette: colour-blind-safe (Okabe-Ito). Every headline is generated from the data.
